theme: Holy living; the coming of the Lord; final exhortations
readingInstruction: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:1-5:28. Paul gives instruction on holy living, brotherly love, the day of the Lord, and a series of brief final exhortations. Notice how many of the commands are short and practical.
settingTheScene: Having celebrated the church and defended his ministry, Paul turns to instruction. He urges the Thessalonians to live in holiness, to love one another, and to work quietly. Then, after the comfort of 4:13-18, he adds a warning and encouragement about the day of the Lord: how to live in the meantime. The letter ends with a rapid-fire list of commands that summarize the Christian life.
observation: “And to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands” (4:11).
“For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (5:2).
“But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation” (5:8).
“For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (5:9).
“Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing” (5:11).
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances” (5:16-18).
“Test everything; hold fast what is good” (5:21).
“He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (5:24).
interpretation:
Chapter 4 opens with a call to please God more and more. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor.” God has called us in holiness, and he gives his Holy Spirit. Regarding brotherly love, Paul says they have been taught by God and are doing it, but to do so more and more. He adds a practical word: “aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.” Some had apparently stopped working in expectation of Christ’s return. Hope does not cancel responsibility.

After the passage on the return of Christ (see the doctrinal pause), chapter 5 addresses “the times and the seasons.” Believers do not need instruction about dates, “for you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, There is peace and security, then sudden destruction will come upon them.” But believers are not in darkness. “For you are all children of light, children of the day.” So the response: “Let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.” The armor is faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. “For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him. Therefore encourage one another and build one another up.”

Then a rapid series of commands. Respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord; esteem them highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves. Admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all. “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.” And the famous three: “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.” These are not a requirement to feel happy always but a settled posture toward God. “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.”

The prayer: “Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.” Holiness is ultimately God’s work. The letter ends: “Pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”
connection: Leviticus 19:2 and 1 Peter 1:15-16 call for holiness. John 13:34-35 gives the new commandment. 2 Thessalonians 3:6-13 deals with idleness. Matthew 24:42-44 compares the coming to a thief. Ephesians 6:13-17 describes the armor. Philippians 4:4-7 is a parallel on joy and prayer. Luke 18:1 and Colossians 4:2 speak of constant prayer. 1 John 4:1 says to test the spirits. Hebrews 13:7, 17 speak of leaders. Philippians 1:6 and Jude 24 assure of God’s keeping.
application:
Pick one of the short commands in 5:14-22 and practice it today.

Practice thanks in all circumstances: list three things for which to give thanks right now, even in hard times.

Ask what “quiet” work you can do faithfully, and do it as for the Lord.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to sanctify you completely and keep you blameless.
Ask him to help you encourage someone with the hope of his coming.
Tell him what you want to hold on to as you wait.
